citation.title: Which Artificial Intelligences Do People Care About Most? A Conjoint Experiment on Moral Consideration
citation.venue: Proceedings of the CHI Conference on Human Factors in Computing Systems, 1–11; supplied arXiv v1 manuscript

reading.source_scope_note: Preregistered-as-reported US conjoint study of relative moral concern toward hypothetical artificial beings. Randomized descriptive features affect which being respondents say it is more wrong to harm. Threat, anthropocentric bias, inferred experience and conditional reciprocity are interpretations, not isolated mediators or evidence of true AI sentience/rights.
access_limits: All supplied manuscript pages and the effect plot inspected. Linked preregistration, full supplements, pretest methods, 20-person follow-up responses and raw data/code were not separately read or executed.
Proceedings metadata verifies publication identity; final-version text was not downloaded or compared with the supplied March arXiv manuscript.

Original referenced mind-perception, robot-abuse, rights, privacy and philosophical sources remain unread unless separately recorded in this corpus; their presence here does not create independent full-text reviews.

study.sample: 1,254 US Prolific signups minus 53 incomplete, 37 attention-check failures and one duplicate = 1,163 analyzed. Mean age 43.9, SD 16.2; 50.7% men, 47.9% women, 73.4% white. Explicitly not nationally representative. Median 8 minutes 40 seconds, payment $1.45.
study.design: Choice-based partial-profile conjoint: each respondent sees seven randomly selected features from eleven, fixed for their thirteen tasks; their order is randomized once and held fixed. Each task pairs two profiles, with feature levels sampled from duplicated-level lists. Matching levels are somewhat less likely than independent uniform selection.
study.features: Autonomy, body, complexity, cooperation, damage avoidance, emotion expression, emotion recognition, intelligence, language, moral judgment and social purpose. Most have three verbal levels; intelligence only somewhat/great; body has none/robotlike/humanlike; purpose has companionship, entertainment, science and business. Features are behavioral descriptions, avoiding explicit claims of feeling pain or emotions.
study.unit: 1,163 respondents × 13 tasks = 15,119 paired choices and 30,238 evaluated profiles. Average 19,242 profile observations per feature are not independent participants. Standard errors are explicitly clustered by participant.
study.outcome: Forced choice: which being would it be more morally wrong for you to harm? No equal-concern or neither option. This estimates relative selection probabilities, not absolute moral standing, legal rights, actual helping or proof of an AI's interests.
study.main_effects: All eleven prespecified directional feature hypotheses supported as reported; individual effects retain significance under the reported 10% FDR correction. Great versus none: moral judgment +23.7 percentage points, emotion expression +22.1, emotion recognition +18.4, cooperation +17.6, damage avoidance +12.2, language +11.3, autonomy +10.6, complexity +9.1. Humanlike body versus no body +15.9; robotlike +6.6. Intelligence great versus somewhat +8.4 is a different baseline.
study.ranking: Moral judgment and emotion expression do not differ detectably, p = .346. Several other pairwise rankings become nonsignificant after correction. Intelligence excluded from formal feature-ranking comparisons due to its different two-level range. Effect size depends on the chosen manipulation range, not an intrinsic universal psychological importance.
study.mechanisms: Authors propose prosociality-contingent concern because AI may be threatening, and anthropocentric bias as one possible explanation for humanlike-body effects. Neither threat nor mind-perception mediation is measured. Other explicit features cannot guarantee all inferred capacities or perceived risk are held constant.
study.follow_up: The main text reports a separate 20-person interpretation follow-up summarized in unread supplements. Roughly half mention humanlike features, but these additional respondents and narrative comments do not independently identify the primary experiment's mechanism.

summary: Add anthropocentric bias as an explicitly proposed evaluative mechanism, distinguished from measured appearance effects and from anthropomorphic attribution. Enrich moral-standing ascription and preserve boundaries for mind attribution, moral typecasting and privacy-paradox references. Do not add eleven feature descriptions as eleven new demonstrated AI behaviors.

findings.definition: Favoring entities in moral evaluation because of their human likeness rather than independently established morally relevant capacities or interests.
findings.origin: Human–robot interaction / social and moral evaluation
findings.ai_evidence_status: Explicitly named possible explanation; humanlike-body description has a randomized choice effect, but a unique anthropocentric mechanism is not experimentally isolated
findings.ai_proposal: Compare an evaluator's judgments of otherwise matched entities whose appearance or description differs in human likeness. Identify actual relevant interests and rights, test whether unsupported resemblance drives the assessment, and distinguish human dignity from optional interface styling. Do not infer machine moral standing merely from a humanlike avatar.
findings.novelty_rationale: Attributing human traits is anthropomorphism; granting greater moral favor because of resemblance is a distinct evaluative preference. A humanlike-body effect is compatible with several mediators and does not prove unfairness or group identification by itself.

evidence.quote: bias based on mere appearance and human-likeness
explanations should be tested in future research

findings.evidence_scope: The authors explicitly offer anthropocentric bias as a possible body-effect account. Table 2 estimates humanlike body versus no body +.159, 95% CI [.135,.184], but that contrast also changes embodiment. Other feature descriptions and a small qualitative follow-up do not uniquely rule out inferred experience, social meaning or harm interpretation.
findings.boundary: Resemblance can be informative without being decisive, and warranted protection may rest on capacities, interests, relationships or human impacts. This study neither proves AI sentience nor makes human rights conditional on appearance, productivity or helpfulness. Do not infer the same mechanism in a model from one preference.

findings.term: Moral consideration varies with hypothetical AI features
findings.definition: Respondents assign relative moral concern to artificial beings by judging which one it would be more wrong to harm.
findings.novelty_rationale: Direct randomized attribute evidence enriches existing standing ascription; the relative harm measure is one aspect, not a new exact synonym for all rights, status or empathy.
findings.evidence_scope: 1,163 respondents make 13 paired choices. All eleven randomized feature hypotheses have effects on relative choice under the stated profile distribution. A forced choice can exist even if a respondent grants both beings little absolute consideration; actual rights or sentience are not established.
findings.boundary: Moral standing, moral agency, perceived capacities, practical harm and legal rights differ. Human concern can be appropriate or mistaken. Its experimental determinants do not settle normative status, authorize manipulation or override affected people's dignity, privacy and safety.

findings.term: Humanlike appearance can affect concern without measured mind attribution
findings.definition: Humanlike cues may lead to inferences about an artificial being, but appearance and attribution of actual human mental capacities are distinct.
findings.novelty_rationale: A body-effect context with an important measurement boundary; the paper does not independently measure its suggested anthropomorphic mediator.
findings.evidence_scope: The body manipulation is descriptive rather than a live robot encounter. Mind attribution is discussed as a possible explanation, while behavioral feature descriptions can lead people to infer additional mental states. This is conceptual/interpretive evidence, not a separate validated attribution scale or a causal mediation result.
findings.boundary: Humanlike styling does not guarantee believed consciousness, safe interaction or ethical correctness. Displayed emotion, inferred feeling and actual experience differ. Designing distress-inducing dependence or falsely claiming a machine needs care is not justified by increased concern scores.

findings.term: Emotion expression and experience attribution must be separated
findings.definition: Described emotional behavior can be taken as evidence of experience, but the study avoids directly asserting subjective capacities.
findings.novelty_rationale: Boundary prevents treating the measured emotion-expression effect as a direct test of sentience attribution or actual feeling.

evidence.quote: avoid asserting the presence of such capacities

findings.evidence_scope: The authors intentionally define features functionally so respondents can interpret them with or without belief in AI minds. Post-task possibility questions about pain/pleasure are exploratory and not analyzed as mediators in the main results. Boundary-only note does not fill a paper gap for experience attribution.
findings.boundary: A claim, expression or damage-avoidance behavior is not sufficient proof of subjective feeling. Both moral concern without mind attribution and inferred minds without genuine consciousness are possible; the present design does not resolve their prevalence.

findings.term: Prosocial agency cues do not automatically exclude patient concern
findings.definition: An artificial being described as making moral judgments can also receive greater concern about being harmed.
findings.novelty_rationale: A boundary on overextending the existing agent/patient opposition; this is not a direct moral-typecasting test with measured agency and patiency mediators.

evidence.quote: Moral judgment: To a great extent

findings.evidence_scope: Moral-judgment and cooperation descriptions increase relative concern in this conjoint. Those are cues, not actual moral-agency scores, and beliefs about experience are not simultaneously identified. The result cannot establish or refute a universal typecasting mechanism.
findings.boundary: Being capable, friendly or useful does not mean an entity has or lacks moral standing. Actual moral patients need not be cooperative or able to reciprocate; human dignity is not contingent on prosocial performance.

findings.term: Stated moral preferences are not demonstrated protective behavior
findings.definition: The paper uses the privacy paradox as an analogy for why stated preferences may not predict real-world behavior.
findings.novelty_rationale: Reference-context boundary only. The current experiment measures neither privacy concern nor disclosure and supplies no new privacy-paradox result.
findings.evidence_scope: The limitations cite a privacy-behavior review to motivate external-validity caution. No original privacy experiment, behavior gap or real-world robot protection is observed; this does not increase selected-paper coverage.
findings.boundary: A hypothetical concern can still matter, but neither preference nor a stated-versus-actual gap is automatically irrational. Do not claim subjects protected, donated to or harmed an AI merely because they selected a profile.

methodological_limits: The supplied version is an arXiv v1 manuscript preceding the verified CHI conference publication. DOI identity does not prove the final proceedings text is identical; no final-version differences are invented or ruled out.
The paper reports preregistration and linked materials, but those records were not independently opened or dated. Do not describe every analytic choice as independently verified prespecified work.
The sample is US-only and explicitly not nationally representative. Demographic resemblance on a few margins does not justify global, population or cross-cultural prevalence claims.

Each person makes thirteen paired forced choices; 30,238 profiles are not independent people. The authors explicitly cluster standard errors at participant level. Repeated profile rows and within-pair dependence should be assessed within that design, not dismissed as ignored replication.

Seven of eleven features are randomly selected per respondent and fixed across their tasks. Effects average over this partial-profile design and level distribution. Unshown attributes may be inferred, and unrealistic combinations may affect interpretation.

Feature levels are drawn without replacement from a list containing each twice, making pairwise matches less likely than independent uniform draws. The AMCE is conditional on that assignment design; the supplement's identification diagnostics are not read here.

No equal, both or neither response is offered. Even a respondent granting no absolute standing must choose one. Relative wrongness-of-harm choices cannot establish universal acceptance of AI rights or the size of absolute moral concern.

One moral-consideration item may reflect the action imagined, property damage, owner interests, a sentient target or discomfort with aggression. A humanlike physical body and disembodied software may evoke different kinds of harm, not only different intrinsic status.

The twenty-person follow-up is reported descriptively in the main text but its raw answers and methods are in unread supplements. It supports an interpretation check, not proof every primary respondent used one meaning or causal mechanism.

Abstract verbal features have different ranges and meanings. A great-extent contrast in emotion recognition is not physically equivalent to a great-extent contrast in complexity; effect rankings depend on chosen baselines. Intelligence's somewhat-to-great contrast is deliberately excluded from formal rankings.

Moral judgment and emotion expression have the two largest point estimates; humanlike body is in the next group. The abstract's broad body/prosociality wording must not be turned into body always being the largest effect.

Many pairwise differences are nonsignificant or lose significance with multiple-testing adjustment. Individual feature hypotheses retain significance under the reported 10% false-discovery-rate correction, which is not the same as a 5% familywise guarantee or every rank being settled.

Moral judgment and emotion recognition are not inherently prosocial in every implementation. The paper's grouping may reflect inferred benevolence, competence or threat reduction, none measured as a mediator. Generic described autonomy is not actual operational independence.

Having a humanlike body versus no body changes both appearance and embodiment. Robotlike-body comparison helps scope the contrast but does not by itself isolate group favoritism, mind attribution or a unique anthropocentric bias.

Threat and positive-intention explanations are discussion hypotheses. The design does not manipulate perceived threat, identify retaliation/reciprocity as a mediator or prove concern is only granted to useful AI.

The paper deliberately distinguishes behavioral expression from felt emotions. Damage avoidance, language, self-protective behavior and a moral-judgment description cannot establish sentience, pain or authentic moral agency.

The result is a human perception effect, not evidence a model favors humanlike entities or suffers when shut down. Evaluating an AI analogue requires a separate matched protocol and justified normative criteria.

Humanlike design can improve some interactions and worsen abuse or dependence in other settings. No live interaction, actual robot abuse, bystander safety, reduced damage or enduring bond is tested here.

Recommendations to evoke reactions matching an AI's true moral status presuppose an unresolved status question. Human welfare, autonomy, honest capability disclosures and authorized oversight remain independent constraints on design.

Cited Replika distress, robot empathy, privacy paradox and rights studies are secondary. A background finding cannot fill a source gap for a behavior not tested here. Humanlike appearance, moral concern, empathy and legal protection are distinct constructs.

External preregistration, pretest study, sensitivity analyses, corrected pairwise tests, raw data and code were not independently reviewed or reproduced. A linked supplement's existence is not a completed read.

cross_paper_learning.finding: A social ascription of standing, robot-directed empathy and a philosophical justification of rights are separate. This experiment supplies relative judgment evidence without establishing the consciousness or rights discussed by the conceptual source.

Emotion cues, humanlike form and inferred experience can affect moral concern through different routes. Neither observer choices nor a model of harm aversion directly proves machine feelings or isolates a unique process.

Identity threat and positive affect are measured or hypothesized constructs with distinct evidence requirements. A favorable service attitude is not the same outcome as concern about harming an artificial being.

Population judgments and their predictors remain descriptive. More agreement or concern does not create normative truth, and human rights should not be made contingent on an interface's attractiveness or utility.

deferred.reason: Retain as the author's proposed interpretation within standing ascription, not a separately established reciprocal motive. Threat, benevolence and conditionality are not isolated mediators.
Operationalized profile descriptions, not eleven newly discovered behaviors. Autonomy, emotion expression/recognition and damage avoidance also do not establish real subjective capacities.
Related theoretical explanations but no species comparison or direct identification measure. Do not merge them as exact synonyms with the explicitly proposed appearance-based anthropocentric bias.
A background research agenda, not a measured temporal expansion or newly defined response in this article. Original dedicated source needed.

deferred.term: Robot abuse reduction / user emotional obligation
deferred.reason: Possible design outcomes and risks discussed through other studies; no actual intervention or behavior is tested here.

limitations: One explicitly named hypothesis added with measurement and normative limits. Existing moral-standing coverage strengthened; three boundary-only notes do not fill source gaps. No AI feeling, universal legal right, enforced moral reciprocity or automatic normative link inferred.
